terms.def: Software trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next word. That simple trick, at enormous scale, lets it write, summarise, translate and work through problems.
The instruction you give an AI. Give it context, a goal and an example, and the work you get back improves dramatically.
When AI states something false with full confidence, like an invented statistic, quote or court case. Check anything you plan to rely on.
The small chunks of text an AI reads and writes, roughly three-quarters of a word in English. Prices and limits are counted in tokens.
How much an AI can hold in mind at once. Today that ranges from a few pages to several books.
An AI that takes actions, not just answers: browsing, filling forms, running code and working through steps toward a goal you set.
Extra training on a narrower set of examples, so a general model gets better at one specific job.
Retrieval-augmented generation. The AI looks up your documents before it answers, so the answer is grounded in your data.
AI that works with more than text: it can read images, listen to audio and watch video.
Running a trained model to get an answer. Training is school; inference is the job.
Everything a model learned from. Its gaps become the model's blind spots.
The internal settings a model adjusts while learning. A rough measure of size, but bigger is not always better.
The chip that powers AI. Designed for video games, now the most fought-over hardware on earth.
A model whose trained settings are published, so any company can run and adapt it on its own servers.
Rules and filters that stop an AI from doing what it shouldn't, from leaking data to giving dangerous advice.
Making sure AI systems pursue the goals people actually intend, not a literal or twisted version of them.
A standard test for comparing AI models. Useful, but models can be tuned to ace the test.
A model that works through a problem step by step before answering. Slower, but much better on hard problems.
Turning text into numbers so a computer can measure how similar two ideas are. The engine behind smart search.
AI that creates new text, images, audio, video or code, rather than only sorting or predicting.
An AI assistant built into a tool you already use, working beside you rather than replacing you.
Data generated by AI to train or test other systems when real data is scarce or private.
AI-made video, image or voice designed to look like a real person. Verify before you share.
A short document explaining what a model was built for, how it was tested and where it falls short.
A setting for randomness. Low gives predictable answers; high gives more varied, creative ones.
Building software by describing what you want in plain language and letting AI write the code.
Artificial general intelligence: AI that can do most intellectual work a person can. Experts disagree on when, and on what it even means.
A country building its own models, data and computing power instead of depending on foreign ones. The IndiaAI Mission is India's version.
The Government of India's platform for AI translation and speech across Indian languages.
Designing a process so a person reviews or approves AI output before it counts.
Software that does things we'd normally call intelligent: understanding language, recognising images, making predictions or decisions.
Teaching computers by example instead of rules. Show a system enough examples and it learns the pattern itself.
Machine learning using neural networks with many layers. It's the engine behind almost every AI breakthrough of the past decade.
Maths loosely inspired by the brain: layers of connected nodes that adjust themselves as they learn from data.
The 2017 design behind today's chatbots. It lets a model weigh how every word in a passage relates to every other word.
A large, general-purpose model trained on broad data, which companies then adapt for specific jobs.
A compact model that's cheaper and faster to run, often good enough for focused tasks and able to run on a phone or laptop.
Background instructions given to an AI before your conversation starts. It sets its role, tone and rules.
Hiding instructions for an AI inside content it reads, like a web page or email, to make it do something unintended.
A cleverly worded prompt that tricks an AI into ignoring its safety rules.
Giving the AI a few examples of what you want before asking. Often the quickest way to better results.
Asking AI to do a task with no examples at all, relying only on what it already learned.
Getting AI to work through a problem step by step before answering. It improves accuracy on tricky questions.
When an AI can call other software, like a calculator, search engine or your calendar, to get a job done.
Application programming interface: a doorway that lets one piece of software talk to another. It's how apps plug into AI models.
Software whose code anyone can read, use and modify. In AI the term is often stretched to cover open-weight models.
The process where a model learns from data by adjusting its internal settings, millions or billions of times.
When a model memorises its training examples so closely that it does badly on anything new.
When an AI system treats groups of people unfairly because of skewed data or design choices.
How well we can understand why an AI made a decision. It matters most for loans, hiring and healthcare.
Using AI in ways that are fair, safe, transparent and accountable. Increasingly a board-level topic.
Where your data is physically stored and processed. Some industries and countries require it to stay within borders.
Tying an AI's answer to trusted sources, like your documents or today's data, so it doesn't make things up.
The date after which an AI model has no built-in knowledge. Anything newer needs search or your input.
How long you wait for an AI's response. Low latency matters for voice assistants and live customer chats.
The raw processing power needed to train and run AI. Today it's one of the scarcest resources in tech.
A building full of servers that store data and run software, including AI. The new factories of the digital economy.
Tensor Processing Unit: Google's own chip designed specifically to train and run AI models.
AI that runs on your phone or laptop instead of in the cloud. Faster, works offline and keeps data private.
Shrinking a model by storing its numbers with less precision, so it runs faster and fits on smaller devices.
Training a small model to imitate a big one, keeping much of the skill at a fraction of the cost.
A database that stores meaning as numbers, so AI can find related ideas instead of exact keyword matches.
Search that understands what you mean, not just the words you type.
The AI that suggests what to watch, buy or read next, based on your behaviour and people like you.
The field of AI that teaches machines to see: recognising faces, reading scans, spotting defects on a production line.
Optical character recognition: turning text in photos or scans into editable text.
AI that turns spoken words into text. The first step in every voice assistant.
AI that turns written text into natural-sounding speech, now in many Indian languages.
Recreating a person's voice from a short sample. Useful for dubbing, risky for fraud.
The technique behind most AI image tools. It starts from random noise and refines it, step by step, into a picture.
AI that generates video clips from a written description.
Hidden markers added to AI-generated content so it can later be identified as machine-made.
A tamper-evident label attached to images and video that records how they were made and edited.
Images, audio or video created or altered by AI.
Alan Turing's 1950 test: can a machine hold a conversation you can't tell apart from a human's?
AI built to do one specific job well, like translation or fraud detection. Almost all AI today is narrow.
A hypothetical AI far smarter than humans in nearly every area. The subject of much of the AI safety debate.
The field focused on making sure AI systems behave as intended and don't cause harm, now or as they get more capable.
Deliberately trying to break or misuse an AI system to find its weaknesses before others do.
Tests that measure how well an AI performs on the tasks you actually care about.
Training AI by rewarding good outcomes and penalising bad ones, so it learns through trial and error.
Reinforcement learning from human feedback: people rate AI answers, and the model learns to give the kind people prefer.
Learning from labelled examples, like thousands of emails each marked 'spam' or 'not spam'.
Finding patterns in data that has no labels, like grouping customers by behaviour.
Data that's been tagged with the right answer, used to teach supervised models.
A collection of data used to train or test an AI model.
The billions of numbers a model learns during training. In effect, they are the model.
A cap on how many requests you can send to an AI service in a given time.
Linking apps and steps so routine work runs by itself, increasingly with AI handling the judgement calls in between.
Tools that let you build AI-powered apps and automations without writing code.
Shared digital rails, like Aadhaar and UPI, that anyone can build on. India's model is studied worldwide.
Coordinating several AI tools or agents so they work together on a bigger task.
Several AI agents, each with a role, working together, like a researcher, a writer and a checker.
A feature that lets an AI remember facts about you across conversations, so you don't repeat yourself.
AI that reads text, like reviews or tweets, and judges whether the tone is positive, negative or neutral.
Sorting things into categories, like routing customer emails to the right team.
Spotting things that don't fit the pattern, like a suspicious transaction or a faulty machine reading.
Using past data to predict future numbers, like demand, sales or cash flow.
Using AI to make people better at their jobs, rather than replacing them.
When employees use AI tools their company hasn't approved. Common, and a data-security headache.
Knowing enough about AI to use it well, spot its mistakes and make good decisions about it.
A reusable prompt with blanks to fill in. Turns one good prompt into a repeatable system.
Carefully choosing what information to give an AI so it has exactly what it needs to do the job well.
A public ranking of AI models by benchmark scores. Useful, but test on your own tasks too.
The finding that AI models get predictably better as you add more data, compute and size.
Skills that seem to appear suddenly once AI models reach a certain size, like basic reasoning.
A period when hype fades and funding for AI dries up. There were major ones in the 1970s and late 1980s.
Gordon Moore's observation that chip transistor counts roughly double every two years, driving decades of cheaper computing.
AI that plans and carries out multi-step tasks toward a goal, rather than just answering one question.

prompts.prompt: Here's my product and audience: [details]. Write 10 ad headlines, rank them by which would stop a busy Indian professional mid-scroll, and explain your top three.
Here are this month's numbers against budget: [paste]. Write variance commentary a CEO can read in 60 seconds. Flag anything that needs a question, not an explanation.
Rewrite this job description so it is clear, inclusive and half the length: [paste].
I'm meeting [company] next week. Based on public information, list their likely priorities this year and three sharp questions I should ask.
Act as a sceptical board member. Here's my plan: [paste]. Ask me the five hardest questions you can.
Interview me one question at a time about a task I do every week. Then tell me which parts AI could do and which need me.
Turn these messy notes into a step-by-step SOP with owners and checkpoints: [paste].
Here are 20 customer complaints: [paste]. Group them into themes, count each one, and suggest one fix per theme.
Here's my draft: [paste]. Don't rewrite it. Show me the three weakest sentences and explain why.
Summarise this contract in plain English, then list every clause that creates an obligation for us, with deadlines: [paste]. Verify with your lawyer.
Explain [concept] as if I'm a smart 15-year-old. Then explain it again at expert level.
I'm nervous about sending this email: [paste]. Tell me how the reader might take it, and suggest a calmer version.
Quiz me on [topic] with five questions, one at a time. Explain anything I get wrong.
Here are my team's recurring meetings: [paste]. Which ones could become a written update instead?
Translate this message into Hindi and Marathi with a casual tone, then translate it back to English so I can check the meaning: [paste].
Before you answer, ask me three questions that would make your answer better. Here's what I need: [task].
Build a simple bad, base and good scenario for [decision]. Show the assumptions in a table I can edit.
I'm stuck on this decision: [details]. Argue for each option as strongly as you can, then tell me what information would settle it.
Write a follow-up to a client who said 'let me think about it'. Give me three versions: gentle, direct and value-add.
Draft a one-page AI use policy for a 50-person company: what's encouraged, what's not allowed and what needs approval.
Turn this article into a LinkedIn post, a five-post thread and a 60-second video script: [paste].
Here's our process: [steps]. Where are delays and handoffs most likely to break, and why?
Summarise this document in five bullets, then tell me what it doesn't say that I'd want to know: [paste].
Write a two-minute talk for my team on why we're adopting AI. Be honest about what changes and what doesn't.
Here's our brand and audience: [details]. Give me five campaign ideas that would only work in India, and explain the cultural insight behind each.
Rewrite this product description in three tones: premium, playful and no-nonsense: [paste]. Tell me which suits our audience best and why.
Act as a sceptical customer. Read this landing page copy: [paste]. List the five questions or doubts that would stop you from buying.
Turn this one idea into a week of content: two LinkedIn posts, three reel hooks and one email subject line: [idea].
Here are our last 20 campaign results: [paste]. What patterns separate the winners from the losers?
Explain this balance sheet to a non-finance manager in under 200 words, and flag the one number they should worry about: [paste].
Here's our expense data for the quarter: [paste]. Find three places we could save at least 10 percent, and the risk of cutting each.
Draft a polite but firm reminder to a client whose invoice is 45 days overdue. Keep the relationship warm.
Act as a sceptical investor. Here's our financial plan: [paste]. Which three assumptions would you challenge first?
Here's my pitch: [paste]. Rewrite it so the first sentence is about the customer's problem, not our product.
A prospect said our price is too high. Give me five ways to respond that focus on value, not discounts.
Turn these rough call notes into a clean CRM entry and a follow-up email: [paste].
Role-play a tough procurement manager. I'll try to close a deal for [product]. Push back the way a real buyer would.
Write five interview questions that test how a candidate uses AI in their work, with what a strong answer sounds like.
Here's our employee survey feedback: [paste]. Summarise the top three themes and one quick win for each.
Draft a warm, clear onboarding checklist for a new hire's first week in a [role] position.
Help me prepare for a difficult conversation with a team member about [issue]. Give me an opening line and three likely reactions with responses.
Here's our process: [steps]. Which steps could an AI agent handle end to end, and which need a person?
Create a simple weekly checklist for [process] that a new team member could follow without help.
Here's a supplier's email: [paste]. Summarise what they're committing to, what's vague, and what I should ask them to confirm.
Write a reply to this angry customer that apologises sincerely, fixes the issue and doesn't sound scripted: [paste].
Here are our 15 most common questions: [paste]. Turn them into a clear, friendly FAQ.
Translate this support reply into Hindi and Tamil, keeping it warm and simple: [paste].
Here's a decision I need to make: [details]. Run a pre-mortem: imagine it failed a year from now and tell me the most likely reasons.
Write a one-page memo to my team explaining [change], covering what's changing, why, and what stays the same.
Act as my executive coach. Ask me five questions, one at a time, to help me prioritise next quarter.
Here are my team's goals: [paste]. Which ones conflict with each other, and how would you resolve it?
Summarise this long report into a 60-second briefing for the board: [paste].
Compare these two versions of a contract and list every change in plain English: [paste both]. Verify with your lawyer.
Explain what this clause means for us in simple terms, and what could go wrong: [paste]. Always confirm with your lawyer.
Here's my article: [paste]. Suggest five headlines: one curious, one bold, one practical, one emotional, one with a number.
Act as a tough editor. Cut this draft by 30 percent without losing any key idea: [paste].
Turn this podcast transcript into a 300-word blog post with three key takeaways: [paste].
I want to write about [topic]. Give me five angles nobody else is taking, with an opening line for each.
Explain [topic] using an analogy from cricket, then quiz me with three questions.
Make me a one-week study plan for [exam or subject], with 45 minutes a day and a short test at the end.
Here are my notes: [paste]. Turn them into ten flashcards with a question on the front and answer on the back.
Read my essay and tell me where my argument is weakest. Don't rewrite it: [paste].
Here's my to-do list: [paste]. Sort it into do today, schedule, delegate and drop, and explain your choices.
I have a big task I keep avoiding: [task]. Break it into steps that each take under 15 minutes.
Explain the pros and cons of [decision] like a friend who knows the topic well, then tell me what you'd do.
Rewrite this message so it's half the length and twice as clear: [paste].
I'm going to a meeting about [topic]. Give me five smart questions to ask and three terms I should understand first.
Here's a news article: [paste]. What's the key fact, what's opinion, and what's missing?
Help me plan a weekend in [city] for [people] on a budget of [amount], with one surprising local experience.
I'll describe my week. Find the three biggest time-wasters and suggest one fix for each: [describe].
Give me a 10-minute daily routine to learn [skill] over the next month, with one small goal per week.
Act as a fact-checker. Here's a claim I saw online: [claim]. What would I need to check to know if it's true?
Write three versions of a reply to this email: one yes, one no, one 'not now': [paste].
I'm feeling stuck on [problem]. Ask me questions one at a time until we find the real issue.
Turn this voice note transcript into a clean summary with action items: [paste].
Compare [option A] and [option B] in a simple table: cost, effort, risk and payoff. Then recommend one.
Act as a seed investor. Here's my pitch: [paste]. What are the three questions you'd ask that I'm not ready for?
Here's my business idea: [idea]. Who are the first 100 customers, and where exactly would I find them?
Write a one-paragraph description of my startup that a 12-year-old would understand: [details].
List ten tasks in my business I could hand to AI tools this month, starting with the easiest.
Audit our brand voice. Here are five recent posts: [paste]. Describe the voice in three words and flag anything off-brand.
Build a simple monthly budget template for a small team, with categories and a column for notes.
Rewrite this policy so it reads like a helpful guide, not a legal document: [paste].
Help me write a clear escalation guide: who to call, when, and what to say, for [type of problem].
I'm presenting [topic] to senior leaders. Predict the three toughest questions and draft crisp answers.
Before I send this, check it for tone, typos and anything that could be misread: [paste].
Summarise this long document in five bullets, then list three questions I should ask its author: [paste].
Pretend you're me a year from now. What would you thank me for starting today, related to [goal]?
Explain how [technology] works, then tell me one way I could use it at work this week.
Give me ten post ideas about AI for managers that aren't about tools, with a hook for each.
Write a cold email to [role] at [company type] that's under 100 words and asks for nothing but a reply.
Here's a complaint thread: [paste]. What went wrong in our process, not just in this case?
Draft a short note thanking my team for [achievement] that's specific, not generic.
Help me say no to this request politely while keeping the relationship strong: [paste].
Turn this messy brainstorm into a structured plan with goals, steps, owners and dates: [paste].
Explain the difference between [concept A] and [concept B] with two everyday examples each.
Draft a simple one-page AI policy for my startup: what's encouraged, what needs approval, what's off-limits.
Write five WhatsApp messages for a festive offer that feel personal, not spammy: [offer details].
Here are two vendor quotes: [paste]. Compare total cost, hidden costs and risks, then recommend one.
I'll paste a long email thread. Tell me who wants what, what's been decided and what's still open: [paste].

quiz.q: AI chatbots search the internet every time they answer you.
quiz.why: Many answer from what they learned in training. Some can search the web, but only when that feature is switched on.

quiz.q: AI can confidently invent facts, sources and quotes.
quiz.why: It's called hallucination. Always check anything you'll rely on.

quiz.q: You need to know how to code to get real value from AI.
quiz.why: For most managers, the value comes from clear instructions and good judgement, not code.

quiz.q: The word 'robot' comes from a Czech play.
quiz.why: Karel Čapek's play R.U.R., written in 1920, introduced it.

quiz.q: The term 'artificial intelligence' was coined in the 2010s.
quiz.why: John McCarthy and colleagues used it in 1955, in their proposal for the 1956 Dartmouth workshop.

quiz.q: GPUs, the chips behind AI, were originally designed for video games.
quiz.why: Their ability to do many calculations at once turned out to be perfect for AI.

quiz.q: Pasting confidential company data into any free AI tool is always safe.
quiz.why: Check each tool's data policy. Business versions usually offer stronger protection.

quiz.q: A computer beat the reigning world chess champion before the year 2000.
quiz.why: IBM's Deep Blue beat Garry Kasparov in 1997.

quiz.q: AI detectors can reliably tell whether text was written by AI.
quiz.why: They produce many false positives. Never use one alone to judge someone's work.

quiz.q: Asking AI to work step by step can improve its answers on hard problems.
quiz.why: Breaking a problem into steps helps models make fewer mistakes.

quiz.q: AI usually replaces whole jobs overnight.
quiz.why: It tends to take over tasks first. Roles change shape over years.

quiz.q: The 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics went to AI pioneers.
quiz.why: John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton won it for foundational work on neural networks.

quiz.q: AI work on predicting protein structures shared a Nobel Prize.
quiz.why: Demis Hassabis and John Jumper shared the 2024 Chemistry prize for AlphaFold, with David Baker.

quiz.q: Bigger AI models always give better answers.
quiz.why: Smaller, specialised models often beat bigger ones on narrow tasks, at a fraction of the cost.

quiz.q: Alan Turing proposed a test for machine intelligence in 1950.
quiz.why: He described it in his paper 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence'.

quiz.q: ChatGPT launched to the public in November 2022.
quiz.why: It reached an estimated 100 million users within about two months.

quiz.q: AI data centres use a lot of electricity.
quiz.why: They are one of the fastest-growing sources of power demand worldwide.

quiz.q: Lawyers have been penalised for submitting fake case citations invented by AI.
quiz.why: It has happened in several countries. Always verify citations at the source.

quiz.q: India has a government platform for AI translation across Indian languages.
quiz.why: It's called Bhashini.

quiz.q: AI models know about events right up to today by default.
quiz.why: Each model has a training cutoff. Without search, it doesn't know what happened after that.

quiz.q: The 'GPT' in ChatGPT stands for Generative Pre-trained Transformer.
quiz.why: Generative because it creates text, pre-trained on huge amounts of text, and built on the transformer design.

quiz.q: The transformer, the design behind most modern chatbots, was introduced in a 2017 Google research paper.
quiz.why: The paper was called 'Attention Is All You Need'. Almost every major language model since builds on it.

quiz.q: AI chatbots remember every conversation you've ever had with them by default.
quiz.why: Most only see the current conversation, unless a memory feature is switched on.

quiz.q: Language models read text in small chunks called tokens, not whole words.
quiz.why: A token is often part of a word. Prices and limits are counted in tokens.

quiz.q: A chatbot always gives exactly the same answer to the same question.
quiz.why: Most add a little randomness, so wording and even content can vary between tries.

quiz.q: ELIZA, one of the first chatbots, was built in the 1960s.
quiz.why: Joseph Weizenbaum created it at MIT. It mimicked a therapist using simple patterns.

quiz.q: Machine learning means programmers write a rule for every possible situation.
quiz.why: It's the opposite: the system learns patterns from examples instead of following hand-written rules.

quiz.q: Geoffrey Hinton, Yoshua Bengio and Yann LeCun shared the 2018 Turing Award.
quiz.why: They won computing's top prize for their work on deep learning, earning the nickname 'godfathers of AI'.

quiz.q: AI image generators always spell words inside images perfectly.
quiz.why: They've improved a lot, but garbled or misspelt text in images still happens. Check before you publish.

quiz.q: Many AI tools let you choose whether your chats are used to train future models.
quiz.why: Look in the privacy or data settings. Business plans often switch training off by default.

quiz.q: Using AI at work always requires expensive enterprise software.
quiz.why: Many capable tools are free or cheap. Start small and pay only once you see value.

quiz.q: IBM's Watson beat human champions on the US quiz show Jeopardy! in 2011.
quiz.why: It was a landmark moment for computers answering questions asked in everyday language.

quiz.q: AlphaFold predicts the 3D shapes of proteins.
quiz.why: DeepMind's system solved a 50-year-old problem in biology and has helped speed up medical research.

quiz.q: Self-driving taxis with no safety driver already carry paying passengers in some cities.
quiz.why: Robotaxi services operate in several cities, though only in carefully mapped areas.

quiz.q: Chatbots understand meaning exactly the way humans do.
quiz.why: They learn patterns from enormous amounts of text. How much they 'understand' is debated, but it isn't human understanding.

quiz.q: Giving AI more context and detail usually improves its answer.
quiz.why: Who it's for, why you need it and what good looks like all help it hit the mark.

quiz.q: Asking AI to 'act as' a role, like a CFO or a sceptical customer, changes its answers.
quiz.why: Roles shift the focus, vocabulary and level of challenge in the response.

quiz.q: AI tools only work in English.
quiz.why: Leading tools work in dozens of languages, including Hindi and other Indian languages, with varying quality.

quiz.q: An AI 'hallucination' means the AI is seeing images that aren't there.
quiz.why: It means the AI states something false with confidence, like an invented fact or source.

quiz.q: AI can summarise a long report in seconds but can still miss or misstate key points.
quiz.why: Use summaries to get oriented, then check anything you'll act on.

quiz.q: Open-weight models can be run on a company's own servers.
quiz.why: Their trained settings are published, so companies can host them privately.

quiz.q: Training a large AI model takes far more computing power than answering one question.
quiz.why: Training can take months on thousands of chips. A single answer takes seconds.

quiz.q: Once trained, a chatbot automatically learns from every new conversation in real time.
quiz.why: Models are mostly fixed after training. Updates come from new training rounds, not live chats.

quiz.q: Email spam filters are an everyday example of machine learning.
quiz.why: They learn from millions of examples of spam and genuine mail.

quiz.q: Streaming and video recommendations are powered by machine learning.
quiz.why: They learn from what you and similar viewers watch to suggest what's next.

quiz.q: AI can't write computer code.
quiz.why: Coding is one of the things AI does best today. Many developers use it daily.

quiz.q: AI-generated voices can be hard to tell apart from real ones.
quiz.why: That's why a phone call asking for urgent money deserves a second check, even if the voice sounds familiar.

quiz.q: Scammers have used AI-cloned voices to impersonate people on calls.
quiz.why: Agree a family or office code word for urgent requests. It's a simple defence.

quiz.q: The European Union has passed a law specifically regulating AI.
quiz.why: The EU AI Act sets rules based on how risky an AI use is.

quiz.q: India has a national AI programme called the IndiaAI Mission.
quiz.why: It funds shared computing power, datasets and Indian-language models.

quiz.q: Alan Turing called his test for machine intelligence 'the imitation game'.
quiz.why: He described it in 1950. The name later became the title of a film about his life.

quiz.q: Arthur Samuel popularised the term 'machine learning' in 1959.
quiz.why: He built a checkers program that improved by playing against itself.

quiz.q: Deep learning is a type of machine learning that uses many-layered neural networks.
quiz.why: The 'deep' refers to the many layers. It powers most of today's AI.

quiz.q: Neural networks are made of real biological neurons.
quiz.why: They're maths loosely inspired by the brain, running on ordinary computer chips.

quiz.q: An 'AI winter' is a period when interest and funding in AI dropped sharply.
quiz.why: There were major ones in the 1970s and late 1980s, after promises outran results.

quiz.q: AI translation is good enough that legal documents never need a human check.
quiz.why: Translation has improved enormously, but contracts and legal text still need expert review.

quiz.q: Some smaller AI models can run directly on a smartphone without internet.
quiz.why: On-device AI is faster and keeps your data on the phone.

quiz.q: AI can analyse a spreadsheet you upload and point out trends.
quiz.why: It's a quick way to get a first read. Always sanity-check the numbers.

quiz.q: You have to say 'please' and 'thank you' for AI to work.
quiz.why: Politeness isn't required. Clear instructions matter far more.

quiz.q: Showing AI an example of the output you want often improves results.
quiz.why: It's called few-shot prompting. One good example beats a paragraph of description.

quiz.q: An AI agent can take actions like booking or filling in forms, not just answer questions.
quiz.why: Agents work through steps toward a goal. Keep a human approval step for anything important.

quiz.q: Generative AI only makes images.
quiz.why: It creates text, images, audio, video and code.

quiz.q: Chatbots can be tricked by instructions hidden in documents or web pages they read.
quiz.why: It's called prompt injection. Be careful letting AI act on untrusted content.

quiz.q: AI systems can inherit biases from the data they learned from.
quiz.why: If the data is skewed, the output can be too. Review AI-assisted decisions about people carefully.

quiz.q: If an AI sounds confident, it's almost certainly right.
quiz.why: Confidence and accuracy aren't linked in AI. Wrong answers can sound just as sure.

quiz.q: Deepfakes can make people appear to say things they never said.
quiz.why: Check the source before you share a shocking clip, especially around elections or markets.

quiz.q: Robots and AI are the same thing.
quiz.why: Robots are physical machines. AI is software. Some robots use AI, many don't.

quiz.q: Most AI in use today is 'narrow AI', built for specific tasks.
quiz.why: Spam filters, recommendations and translation each do one job well.

quiz.q: Scientists have officially declared that human-level AI, or AGI, has been achieved.
quiz.why: There's no agreed definition or official test, and experts still disagree on when, or whether, it will arrive.

quiz.q: Moore's Law described the number of transistors on a chip roughly doubling every two years.
quiz.why: Gordon Moore's observation helped explain decades of ever-cheaper computing.

quiz.q: NVIDIA started out making graphics chips for gaming.
quiz.why: The same chips turned out to be ideal for training AI.

quiz.q: The 1956 Dartmouth workshop is often called the birthplace of AI as a field.
quiz.why: It brought together the researchers who launched AI as a discipline.

quiz.q: AI can't help with creative work like brainstorming.
quiz.why: It's a strong brainstorming partner for volume and variety. Your taste picks the winner.

quiz.q: Voice assistants like Siri and Alexa use AI to understand spoken requests.
quiz.why: Speech recognition and language understanding both rely on machine learning.

quiz.q: Google Translate switched to neural machine translation in 2016.
quiz.why: The change made translations noticeably more natural almost overnight.

quiz.q: Reading text from photos and scanned documents (OCR) is a form of AI.
quiz.why: Optical character recognition uses pattern recognition to turn images of text into text.

quiz.q: AI can predict the stock market with certainty.
quiz.why: No model can. Markets react to new events nobody can foresee. Be wary of anyone who claims otherwise.

quiz.q: A bigger context window lets AI work with longer documents at once.
quiz.why: It's how much text the AI can keep in view in a single conversation.

quiz.q: Pasting customer phone numbers and passwords into a chatbot is a good way to get better answers.
quiz.why: Never share sensitive personal data or passwords with AI tools unless your company has approved it.

quiz.q: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets AI answer using your own documents.
quiz.why: The AI looks up relevant passages first, then answers from them.

quiz.q: A company must retrain its AI model from scratch every time it adds a new document.
quiz.why: With RAG, new documents can be searched right away without retraining.

quiz.q: Siri first launched on the iPhone in 2011.
quiz.why: It arrived with the iPhone 4S and brought voice assistants to the mainstream.

quiz.q: Multimodal AI can work with text, images and audio together.
quiz.why: You can show it a photo and ask questions about it out loud.

quiz.q: You need a team of data scientists before your company can use AI.
quiz.why: Most everyday AI use needs clear goals and curious people, not a data science team.

quiz.q: A setting called 'temperature' controls how random or creative AI's answers are.
quiz.why: Low temperature gives predictable answers. High gives more varied ones.

quiz.q: Fine-tuning means training an existing model further on specialised examples.
quiz.why: It's how a general model gets better at one specific job.

quiz.q: Google designed its own AI chips, called TPUs.
quiz.why: Tensor Processing Units are built specifically for AI workloads.

quiz.q: Running AI on your own laptop always needs an internet connection.
quiz.why: Smaller open models can run fully offline on a decent laptop.

quiz.q: Reinforcement learning trains AI by rewarding good outcomes.
quiz.why: It's a bit like training with treats. It helped AI master games like Go.

quiz.q: AlphaGo learned partly by playing huge numbers of games against itself.
quiz.why: Self-play let it discover strategies human players had never tried.

quiz.q: Computer vision is the field of AI that helps machines interpret images and video.
quiz.why: It powers face unlock, quality checks in factories and medical scan analysis.

quiz.q: Facial recognition is equally accurate for everyone.
quiz.why: Accuracy has varied across skin tones, ages and genders, which is why its use is closely debated.

quiz.q: Google Search automatically bans any content written with AI.
quiz.why: Google says it focuses on whether content is helpful and original, not on how it was produced.

quiz.q: A chatbot can help you rehearse a difficult conversation before you have it.
quiz.why: Ask it to play the other person. It's a low-stakes way to practise.

quiz.q: AI can reliably tell when someone is lying from their face.
quiz.why: There's no reliable scientific basis for lie detection from facial expressions.

quiz.q: AI models can be 'jailbroken' into ignoring their safety rules.
quiz.why: Cleverly worded prompts sometimes get around safeguards. Companies keep patching them.

quiz.q: The word 'algorithm' comes from the name of the Persian mathematician al-Khwarizmi.
quiz.why: His 9th-century work on calculation gave us both 'algorithm' and 'algebra'.

quiz.q: Ada Lovelace wrote what is often called the first computer program, in the 1840s.
quiz.why: She described how Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine could follow a sequence of instructions.

quiz.q: The Turing Test checks whether a machine can do arithmetic faster than a person.
quiz.why: It asks whether a machine can hold a conversation that's indistinguishable from a human's.

quiz.q: Some AI tools can turn a written description into a working website.
quiz.why: Describe what you want and get a first draft in minutes. Polish still takes a human eye.

quiz.q: AI can't read handwriting.
quiz.why: Modern AI reads handwriting well, even messy notes, though unusual scripts can still trip it up.

quiz.q: AI data centres use large amounts of electricity and water.
quiz.why: Power for computing and water for cooling make AI's environmental footprint a growing debate.

quiz.q: Edge AI means running AI on the device itself rather than in the cloud.
quiz.why: It's faster, works offline and keeps data local.

quiz.q: The AI model that tops a public benchmark is guaranteed to be best for your task.
quiz.why: Benchmarks test general skills. Try models on your own real tasks before deciding.

quiz.q: Andrew Ng co-founded the online learning platform Coursera.
quiz.why: He co-founded it with Daphne Koller in 2012.

quiz.q: Fei-Fei Li led the creation of ImageNet, a dataset that helped spark the deep learning boom.
quiz.why: ImageNet's millions of labelled images became the proving ground for modern computer vision.

quiz.q: Demis Hassabis co-founded DeepMind.
quiz.why: DeepMind was acquired by Google in 2014 and is now Google DeepMind.

quiz.q: Yann LeCun pioneered convolutional neural networks, used in image recognition.
quiz.why: His early work read handwritten digits on bank cheques.

quiz.q: AI will only affect jobs in the technology industry.
quiz.why: It touches marketing, finance, HR, law, healthcare and almost every desk job.

quiz.q: CAPTCHAs were designed to tell humans and computers apart.
quiz.why: The name stands for a 'Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart'.

quiz.q: A neural network's 'weights' are the numbers it adjusts while learning.
quiz.why: Training is the process of nudging billions of these numbers until the outputs get better.

quiz.q: Generative AI tools went mainstream after ChatGPT launched in late 2022.
quiz.why: It became one of the fastest-adopted consumer apps ever.

quiz.q: Aadhaar is an example of India's digital public infrastructure.
quiz.why: Along with UPI and DigiLocker, it's often cited as a base for AI services at population scale.

quiz.q: Sarvam AI is an Indian company building AI for Indian languages.
quiz.why: It's one of several Indian efforts to build models that understand local languages and context.

quiz.q: AI can draft a presentation outline from a few bullet points.
quiz.why: It's a fast way past the blank page. Shape the story yourself.

quiz.q: Being vague in your prompt makes AI more creative and accurate.
quiz.why: Vague prompts get generic answers. Specific goals, audiences and examples get better work.

quiz.q: AI tools can transcribe a meeting and list the action items.
quiz.why: Always check names, numbers and decisions before sending the notes around.

quiz.q: The first AI chatbots in the 1960s used the same technology as today's chatbots.
quiz.why: Early chatbots used hand-written rules. Today's learn from vast amounts of text.
